One framework, not two

In puzzle 5, Kotlin/Native packed your shared code into a framework. Your project has several shared modules. Here's why they should reach Swift as one framework, and what each exported line costs.

  • Puzzle 7: Counting or tracing

    A tracing garbage collector starts from the roots, the references a program always has (local and global variables), follows every reference, and frees whatever it couldn't reach, even objects that point at each other. Reference counting keeps a count of strong references on every object and frees it the moment the count hits zero, but two objects holding each other never reach zero: a cycle it can't free.

The problem

In puzzle 5, your shared code became a framework that Swift imports. Your project has grown: a network module, a database module, a features module. The obvious move is one framework per module, so the iOS app imports three. Why does that go wrong?

See it

Save this diagram as a GIF

The building block

A Kotlin framework isn't only your code: it also carries the Kotlin runtime, the standard library and the garbage collector from puzzle 9. Build three frameworks and the app carries three runtimes, each with its own copy of everything, and Kotlin's docs say using several Kotlin frameworks in one Swift app is limited: a Kotlin type from one framework isn't the same type as the same class in another.

So you ship one umbrella framework: a single framework, with one runtime, that brings in every Kotlin module Swift needs. In Gradle you list which modules it exports to Swift:

binaries.framework { export(project(":network")) }

Exporting has a cost. An exported module comes in with its whole API, even if Swift uses a tiny part of it, and that turns off dead code elimination for it: the step that leaves out compiled code nothing uses, to keep the app small. So export only the modules Swift actually calls; the others still go into the framework, but trimmed to the code that's used.

For distribution, the umbrella framework is usually built as an XCFramework: one bundle holding the selected device and simulator builds you distribute, which the iOS project adds like any other library.

The analogy

One shipping container instead of three: each container comes with its own crane (the runtime), and goods from one container can't be swapped for the same goods from another. And whatever you put on the manifest (the export list) is shipped whole, even the parts nobody ordered.

Check yourself

An app imports two Kotlin frameworks, and both contain the same User class. Swift passes a User from one to the other. What happens?

Not quite. Each framework has its own runtime and its own copy of the class; to Swift they're different types.

Right. Two frameworks, two copies of every type.

Not quite. Where the class came from doesn't help: two frameworks, two types.

Why export only the modules Swift calls, instead of everything?

Not quite. They are compiled in, and trimmed to what's used; only exports come in whole.

Not quite. Swift can read many; the cost is size, since exported code isn't trimmed.

Right. Exports are kept whole; the rest is trimmed.

What's the difference between an umbrella framework and an XCFramework?

Right. What's inside vs which devices.

Not quite. That's the two swapped. Re-read that part ↑

Not quite. One is about which modules are inside; the other about which devices it's built for. Re-read that part ↑

Sources
  • Kotlin docs: Build final native binaries ("Usage of several Kotlin/Native frameworks in a Swift application is limited, but you can create an umbrella framework and export all these modules to it"; "When you export a dependency, it includes all of its API to the framework API. The compiler adds the code from this dependency to the framework, even if you use a small fraction of it. This disables dead code elimination"; "XCFrameworks… gather logic for all the target platforms and architectures in a single bundle")

What you now know

Each Kotlin framework carries its own copy of the Kotlin runtime, and using several in one Swift app is limited. So ship one umbrella framework that exports the modules Swift needs. Every exported module comes in whole, which turns off dead code elimination for it: export only what Swift calls.
